Convention for the Settlement of Investment Disputes6 (the ‘‘ICSID Convention’’) had not been implemented in Pakistan through domestic legislation.7 Business transactions and investment treaties most often include clauses for the settlement of disputes through international arbitration. Reformation and mod- ernisation of Pakistani laws on recognition and enforcement of foreign arbitration agreements and awards was due for a long time.8 At the time of independence from British rule, both Pakistan and India inherited the same arbitration laws, but India ﬁrst enacted the Foreign Awards (Recognition and Enforcement) Act as early as 1961. India has now enacted the Indian Arbitration and Conciliation Act in 1996, which is based on the 1985 UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Arbitration9 (the ‘‘Model Law’’), and consolidates arbitration laws repealing the outdated AA and APC along with the Act of 1961. The 1958 Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards10 (the ‘‘New York Convention’’) succeeded the Geneva Protocol and the Geneva Convention.

Understanding Research with Children and Young People: Introduction A considerable amount of research has been carried out into the lives of children and young people, and some of it has been very influential for policy and practice. It has provided new understanding and raised important questions about widely accepted assumptions across a range of fields, including health, education, social work, and crime. This research has taken many different forms, and there have been intense debates about some aspects of it. These are concerned with how knowledge can be produced and its proper character, the practical value of such knowledge, and the very nature of childhood and youth.

Gascoigne*, David Thomas** and Fiona Kidd*** *University of Southampton **La Trobe University, Melbourne ***Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York Abstract The Bala Hissar was the royal, military and administrative heart of Kabul for a significant period before it was occupied by British forces during the first two Anglo-Afghan wars in the nineteenth century. Despite its archaeological and historical significance, part of the site continues to function as a military base, an expan- sion of which began in 2007 when nine large holes were bulldozed into the site before protests halted the work. This paper details the findings of an archaeological impact assessment undertaken in July 2007, and incorporates an analysis of satellite images documenting further construction in 2009.

A few years earlier, Reshma’s sons had ﬂed to the Pakistan-administered side of Kashmir to escape police persecution because of their alleged role in cross-LOC trafﬁcking. Uri is a garrison town near the Line of Control that separates the two regions of Kashmir under separate Indian and Pakistani control. The erstwhile princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, now divided and under Indian military occupation, stands as a testament to the fraught postcolonial aftermath of the partitioning of India and Pakistan in 1947, which is manifested in the landmark divide, the Line of Control.

CHAPTER 3 The Killable Kashmiri Body The Life and Execution of Afzal Guru ATHER ZIA I hope my forced silence will be heard. —Afzal Guru, in an open letter to his lawyer, Sushil Kumar The motif of the body in the context of violence has been pivotal for tracing the contours of physical power practiced by the sovereign state on its subjects. In order to approach the body as a crucial site on which the multiplicities of state power engage and reproduce the sovereignty of the occupying state, I use the Foucauldian analytic of the “spectacle” to analyze how Kashmiri bodies are constructed as “traitors” to Indian sovereignty and marked as “deviant” and “killable” in the nationalist imaginary. I argue that the spectacle of the killable body is important for the consolidation of the nation- state project of India and for concretizing India’s irrefutable sovereignty over Kashmir. In what follows, I illustrate the creation of the spectacular “killable” Kashmiri body by focus- ing on Mohammad Afzal Guru, a thirty- two- year- old Kashmiri man who was implicated in the armed attack on the Indian Parliament in 2001.

Princely India Re-imagined The princely states of India covered about 40 per cent of the Indian subcontinent at the time of Indian independence, and they collapsed after the departure of the British. This book provides a chronological analysis of the Princely State in colonial times and its post-colonial legacies. Focusing on one of the largest and most impor- tant of these states, the Princely State of Mysore, it offers a novel interpretation and thorough investigation of the relationship of king and subject in South Asia. The book argues that the denial of political and economic power to the king, especially after 1831 when direct British control was imposed over the state administration in Mysore, was paralleled by a counter-balancing multiplication of kingly ritual, rites, and social duties.

The narrative is multifaceted and deeply personal; the text and the photographs spread across time and cities connected by disparate fragments of memory. The essay is presented in ways dictated by loss and grief and the memory of a person rather than as an afterthought. We preserve the jagged edges and fragmentary form of such emotions to reflect the affective and visual response to this loss. PENGUIN BOOKS ICE-CANDY-MAN Distinguished international writer Bapsi Sidhwa lives in America but travels frequently to the Indian subcontinent. She has published five novels: An American Brat, Cracking India, Pakistani Bride, The Crow-Eaters and Ice-Candy-Man, and has been translated into German, French, Italian and Russian. Among her many honours Sidhwa received the Lila Wallace-Reader’s Digest Writer’s Award in 1994, the US National Endowment for the Arts grant in 1994, the Sitara-i- Imtiaz, Pakistan’s national honour in the arts, and the LiBeraturepreis in Germany. It is also about a ‘Large Ocean’, the Indian Ocean world – its peoples, histories and cultures. It casts down a light on the life of an island through what is known not only about the island itself, but also through what is known about the wider Indian Ocean world. It is also about the Indian Ocean world in that it focuses on an island, which, in many senses and dimensions, is not only a model of, but in some respects also a model for wider developments and features of relevance to the Indian Ocean world as a whole.

Based on 1994-2003 fieldwork in Boudha (Kathmandu), Dharamsala and other Himalayan refugee communities, plus interviews with retired CIA officers, the book argues that this 'forgotten war' has been arrested in Tibetan public memory by the politics of nonviolence and the Dalai Lama's exile leadership. Cecilia_Coale_Van_Hollen/Cancer_and_the_.title: Cancer and the Kali Yuga
Cecilia_Coale_Van_Hollen/Cancer_and_the_.author: Cecilia Coale Van Hollen
Cecilia_Coale_Van_Hollen/Cancer_and_the_.summary: Field sites: Palar. ix Seated cross-legged on a soft tan mat made of woven korai grass, with my Blossom Special Notebook and pen in hand, a water bottle by my side, and my mini-recorder perched in the middle of a circle of women, I was leaning in to hear a story about a woman from this village who had died of breast cancer. Except for one teenage girl dressed in an indigo salwar kameez who was sitting on the edge of our circle, the others were all grown women in worn and faded saris of yellow, orange, purple, and green. The heat was intense on that July morning in 2015. The rains had not yet come to northeastern Tamil Nadu.

RENNE Foreword by Annette Weiner "Cloth only wears, it does not die," the paradoxical phrase from a Bùnú Yorùbá prayer, emphasizes the power of cloth as a symbol of continuing social relations and identities in the face of uncertainty and death. The Bùnú Yorùbá people of central Nigeria mark every critical junc- ture in an individual's life, from birthing ceremonies to funeral celebrations, with handwoven cloth. Anthropologist Elisha Renne explains how and why this is so and discusses why handwoven cloth is still valued although it is rarely woven in Bùnú villages today.

Korom's edited volume from the seventh seminar of the International Association for Tibetan Studies (Graz 1995), addressing the cultural, economic and aesthetic politics of the post-1959 Tibetan diaspora. Contributions by Methfessel, Ström, Thargyal, Kalkowski, Klieger, McLagan, Schrempf and Huber treat refugee economic adaptation, monastic institution-building in exile, secularisation, performance politics, hyperreality and Shangri-La, the 'Year of Tibet' in Manhattan, and the reframing of devil dances as world healing. GLYN_WILLIAMS/Seeing_the_State__Governan.title: Seeing the State
GLYN_WILLIAMS/Seeing_the_State__Governan.author: GLYN WILLIAMS
GLYN_WILLIAMS/Seeing_the_State__Governan.summary: Field sites: Lohra. Seeing the State Poor people confront the state on an everyday basis all over the world. But how do they see the state, and how are these engage- ments conducted? This book considers the Indian case where people’s accounts, in particular in the countryside, are shaped by a series of encounters that are staged at the local level, and which are also informed by ideas that are circulated by the government and the broader develop- ment community. Drawing extensively on ﬁeldwork conducted in east- ern India and their broad range of expertise, the authors review a series of key debates in development studies on participation, good governance, and the structuring of political society.

G_C_Sharma_Thakur/The_Lalungs__in.gov.tr.title: The Lalungs

G_C_Sharma_Thakur/The_Lalungs__in.gov.tr.summary: G.C. Sharma Thakur's 1985 monograph on the Tiwas (Lalungs), a plains-and-foothills tribe of central Assam concentrated in Nagaon district and the Hamren subdivision of Karbi Anglong, published by the Tribal Research Institute, Assam. The book covers material culture, life-cycle rites, social institutions, religious beliefs, festivals, language and the Tiwa kingship tradition centred on the Gobha Raja, drawing on the author's fieldwork in Tiwa villages and his interviews with the Gobha Raja and elders. Field sites: Nagaon district (Jagi Bhakatgaon, Barapujia) and Karbi Anglong, Assam. Published Guwahati, 1985.

Gary_Shepherd/The_Economic_Rise_of_Early.author: Gary Shepherd
Gary_Shepherd/The_Economic_Rise_of_Early.summary: Field sites: Model Town. The discovery of America, and that of a passage to the East Indies by the Cape of Good Hope, are the two greatest and most important events recorded in the history of mankind. Their consequences have already been very great: but in the short period of between two and three centuries which has elapsed since these discoveries were made, it is impossible that the whole extent of their consequences can have been seen. What benefits, or what misfortunes to mankind may hereafter result from those great events, no human wisdom can foresee. By uniting, in some measure, the most distant parts of the world, by enabling them to relieve one another's wants, to increase one another's enjoyments, and to encourage one another's industry, their general tendency would seem to be beneficial.

Giuseppe_Tucci/The_Religions_of_Tibet__2.summary: Giuseppe Tucci's authoritative survey of Tibetan religion, originally published in German in 1970 and translated by Geoffrey Samuel. The book traces the first and second diffusions of Buddhism in Tibet, the rise of the Sakya, Kagyu, Nyingma, Geluk and Jonang schools, the doctrinal foundations of Mahayana and Vajrayana, the Bla na med rgyud Tantric process, monastic organisation, the religious calendar, and folk religion (protective deities, soul beliefs, divination), closing with a substantial chapter on the indigenous Bon religion. Giuseppe_Tucci/Tibet__Land_of_Snows__tib.title: These more scientific forms give the uninitiated layman no guidance
Giuseppe_Tucci/Tibet__Land_of_Snows__tib.author: Giuseppe Tucci
Giuseppe_Tucci/Tibet__Land_of_Snows__tib.summary: Giuseppe Tucci's illustrated synthesis of Tibetan civilisation, drawing on his eight scholarly expeditions to Tibet between 1927 and 1948. Chapters cover history, religion (Buddhism and Bon), art, daily life, life-cycle ritual, literature and pre-1959 administration, with particular strength on the monastic art collections at Sakya, Narthang, Shalu, Ngor, Kongkardzong, Reting and Samye. Methodology: a blend of philological, art-historical and field observation, anchored in Tucci's mastery of Tibetan and Sanskrit sources. Field sites: central and western Tibet (especially Sakya, Gyantse, Lhasa, Shigatse) and Ladakh. Translated from Italian; published Elek Books, London, 1967.

The committee toured every province (Bengal, Eastern Bengal and Assam, the United Provinces, Punjab, the North-West Frontier Province, Madras, Bombay, Sind, Central Provinces, Coorg, Ajmer-Merwara, Baluchistan and the cantonments in Native States) and recommended reforms to outstill, distillery, contract-supply and toddy-tax systems, plus duties on imported spirits, wines and beers. Field site: British India as a whole. Published Madras, 1906.

Jamil_Hanifi/Review_Essay__Vending_disto.author: Jamil Hanifi
Jamil_Hanifi/Review_Essay__Vending_disto.summary: Field sites: Kandahār. The destabilization and military occupation of Afghanistan by the United States over the past three decades has triggered the hasty production of a large corpus of writings about the political and socio-cultural dynamics of the country by Euro- American academics, travelers, journalists, and aid and development workers. Anthropologists who have contributed to these writings have become instant ‘authorities’, ‘experts’, ‘specialists’, and ‘old hands’ about the country. Thomas Barﬁeld (aka Thomas Jeﬀerson Barﬁeld III) is one of the most visible members of these groups. He has been referred to as ‘one of America’s foremost authorities on Afghanistan’ and an ‘old Afghanistan hand’ , and has been ‘asked to occasionally advise policymakers’ (p. x).

Jamil_Jan_Kochai/9780593297209__05932972.title: 99 Nights in Logar
Jamil_Jan_Kochai/9780593297209__05932972.author: Jamil Jan Kochai
Jamil_Jan_Kochai/9780593297209__05932972.summary: Jamil Jan Kochai's debut novel, narrated by a 12-year-old Afghan-American boy in 1999 visiting his family's village in Logar province. Field site: Logar Province, Afghanistan — the village of Naw Abad and surrounding terrain. Combines coming-of-age narrative, Pashto folktale, and the inheritance of war. Shortlisted for the 2019 PEN/Hemingway Award.

Jamil_Jan_Kochai/9780735235595__07352355.title: The Haunting of Hajji Hotak and Other Stories
Jamil_Jan_Kochai/9780735235595__07352355.author: Jamil Jan Kochai

Field sites: Logar (Mohammad Agha District), Peshawar, San Joaquin Valley California. Magical-realist explorations of war, memory, and migration. Long-listed for the National Book Award.

Jan_Peter_Hartung/The_Pashtun_Borderland.title: The Pashtun Borderland: A Religious and Cultural History of the Taliban
Jan_Peter_Hartung/The_Pashtun_Borderland.author: Jan Peter Hartung
Jan_Peter_Hartung/The_Pashtun_Borderland.summary: Jan-Peter Hartung's The Pashtun Borderland traces the religious and cultural history of the Pashtun region across the Pakistan-Afghanistan border, situating the Taliban movement within longer Deobandi and Sufi traditions. The book combines archival history with fieldwork in Peshawar and the tribal areas. Field sites: Peshawar, FATA, eastern Afghanistan. Methodology: religious-cultural history. Published 2024 by Hurst.

Javed_Iqbal/A_Study_of_Research_Trends_a.title: A Study of Research Trends at Master Level in Education in the Universities of Punjab
Javed_Iqbal/A_Study_of_Research_Trends_a.author: Javed Iqbal
Javed_Iqbal/A_Study_of_Research_Trends_a.summary: Mazhar Iqbal, Akhtar Ali and Muhammad Javed's documentary analysis of 1,132 Master's-level theses in education submitted between 1988 and 2008 at five Punjab universities — Bahauddin Zakariya University Multan, The Islamia University of Bahawalpur, Government College University Faisalabad, University of the Punjab Lahore, and University of Sargodha. The authors classify each thesis by methodology and topical area, finding heavy concentration in teacher education and severe neglect of guidance and counselling, and recommend a national encyclopedia of educational research. Methodology: content analysis of thesis abstracts. Field sites: educational departments in Multan, Bahawalpur, Faisalabad, Lahore and Sargodha. Published in Bulletin of Education and Research, 2018.

John_Clark/Memoirs_Of_Major-general_Sir_.summary: Field sites: Khyber Agency. THE publication of this volume has been postponed to afford time for the collection of materials for a more complete Life of General IIavelock than has yet appeared. Many valuable documents, in reference more particularly to the campaign of 1857, have only been received from India during the present year; and the compiler is not without hope of obtaining a farther accession of information, which may serve to increase the interest of the work. Should this attempt to do justice to the memory of Havelock be honoured with the encouragement of the public, any addi- tional notices which may be received will be embodied in a subsequent edition. A work of this description, however, published on the sole responsibility, as regards facts and opinions, of one who has not the advantage of military experience, will stand in need of no small indul- gence from professional critics, and he trusts that he will not solicit it in vain.

The cultural landscape was almost medieval in char- acter. Massive vertical windmills in the Hari Rud Valley and the mosaics of carefully tended fields and gardens could both have been described by Arab geographers in the seventh century A.D. The trav- eler also would have seen many karez (or qanat).

Whereas research on the Hindu and Sikh poster traditions has already resulted in several monographs (Vitsaxis 1977; Anton-Warrior 1986; McLeod 1991; Pinney 1 992; Inglis 1 995; Smith 1 995), references to Islamic devotional portraits, depictions of sacred places, poster-calligraphies, and so on are still sketchy and mainly restricted to Egypt (Kriss and Kriss-Heinrich 1960:41-47; Schienerl 1985, 1986). An exception is a recent monograph generally dealing with popular poster-prints in Islam (Centlivres and Centlivres-Demont 1 997).

Karl_Jettmar/Antiquities_of_Northern_Pak.title: Antiquities of Northern Pakistan
Karl_Jettmar/Antiquities_of_Northern_Pak.author: Karl Jettmar
Karl_Jettmar/Antiquities_of_Northern_Pak.summary: Karl Jettmar's Antiquities of Northern Pakistan documents pre-Islamic rock carvings and inscriptions along the upper Indus and its tributaries from Chilas to Hunza, arguing that the region was a long-standing crossroads between South, Central, and East Asian religious traditions. The volumes catalogue Buddhist, Zoroastrian, Hindu, and shamanic motifs at sites including Hodar, Sazin, and Thalpan. Field sites: Chilas, Hodar, Sazin, Thalpan along the upper Indus, Pakistan. Methodology: archaeological survey and epigraphic analysis. Published 1989 onward by Philipp von Zabern.

Karl_Jettmar/Cultures_of_the_Hindukush__.title: Cultures of the Hindukush
Karl_Jettmar/Cultures_of_the_Hindukush__.author: Karl Jettmar

Contributors include Schuyler Jones, Lennart Edelberg, and Jettmar himself. Field sites: Nuristan, Chitral, Hunza, Gilgit. Methodology: collected ethnographic and archaeological essays. Published 1974 by Franz Steiner.

Karl_Jettmar/The_Voice_Of_The_Nightingal.title: The Voice of the Nightingale: A Personal Account of the Wakhi Culture in Hunza
Karl_Jettmar/The_Voice_Of_The_Nightingal.author: Karl Jettmar
Karl_Jettmar/The_Voice_Of_The_Nightingal.summary: Karl Jettmar's The Voice of the Nightingale is a personal ethnographic account of Wakhi-speaking Ismaili communities in upper Hunza, drawing on decades of fieldwork in Gojal. The book documents Wakhi oral poetry, kinship, and seasonal pastoral movement. Field site: upper Hunza Valley (Gojal), Gilgit-Baltistan, Pakistan. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with Wakhi informants. Published 1996.

Laura_A_Ring/Zenana__Everyday_Peace_in_a.title: Zenana: Everyday Peace in a Karachi Apartment Building
Laura_A_Ring/Zenana__Everyday_Peace_in_a.author: Laura A Ring
Laura_A_Ring/Zenana__Everyday_Peace_in_a.summary: Laura A. Ring's ethnography of a multi-ethnic, middle-class high-rise apartment building in Karachi, where she lived with her Pakistani in-laws. Argues that peace between Sindhi, Mohajir, Pashtun, and Punjabi households is the product of relentless daily labor performed by women in the zenana — visiting, borrowing, lending, and managing male anger. Links the psychological idiom of 'tension' to anthropological theories of exchange, showing that ethnic difference is borne and sustained rather than resolved. A canonical urban ethnography of Pakistan's largest city. Field site: Karachi.

Louis_Dupree/Deh_Morasi_Ghundai__A_Chalc.author: Louis Dupree

Magnus_Marsden/Muslim_village_intellectu.author: Magnus Marsden
Magnus_Marsden/Muslim_village_intellectu.summary: Field sites: Chitrāl District. Today more than ever before, there is a need for sophisti- cated anthropological insight into the forms of individual and collective self-transformation for which the problem- atic term ‘Islamization’ has come to be widely used. Among both academics and popular commentators, the ‘Islamizing’ process is often represented as a matter of irresistible pressures to embrace a single, all-powerful model of moral and spiritual perfection based on behav- ioural codes derived either from Qur’anic texts or from the teachings of Islamic jurists and other authorities. So-called village Muslims are often said to be either straightfor- wardly resistant or meekly submissive and uncritical in their responses to the calls of self-styled Islamic purists and reformers. In this article I present a very different account of the processes of Islamization in Chitral, a region of northern Pakistan which has been profoundly affected by movements of both local and global Islamic activism, including the rise and fall of the Taliban regime in nearby Afghanistan, and the effects of regional conflict involving the region’s majority Sunni and Shia Ismaili sectarian communities.1 For the last seven years my…

Magnus_Marsden/Talking_the_talk__Debatin.title: Talking the talk
Magnus_Marsden/Talking_the_talk__Debatin.author: Magnus Marsden
Magnus_Marsden/Talking_the_talk__Debatin.summary: Field sites: Chitrāl District. Having watched the political history of Afghanistan unfold from the verdant villages of Chitral, northern Pakistan, in 2005 I made the first of the five fieldwork visits to Afghanistan on which this article is based. In Chitral I spent much time chatting to Dari-speaking Afghan refu- gees, many of whom had lived in Chitral since the start of violent conflict in Afghanistan in 1979. My fieldwork in Chitral focused on the complexity of local conceptions of Muslim virtuosity, and the centrality to these of the dis- play of critical intellect. My Khowar-speaking Chitrali friends took great pleasure in hotly debating ideas with one another – lively discussion ensured that village life did not stagnate but, rather, was made intellectually stimu- lating; being a skilled participator in such exchanges was also held to be a marker of great personal prestige, a sign of the accomplishment of ‘fully realised humanity’ (pura insaniyat) .

US AND PAKISTAN Mariam Durrani Abstract In this article, I oﬀer the “imperial optic” as an ethnographic approach to observe and analyze the ongoing impact of US empire on Pakistani-origin youth. Drawing from twenty-four months of ethno- graphic ﬁeldwork in Lahore, New York City, and online (2013–19) with two groups of participants— (1) Pakistani Diaspora Muslim students at a public college in the United States and (2) Pakistani Pashtun Muslim scholarship students at a private university in Pakistan—I analyze how US war poli- cies shaped student access and mobility within each respective institution of higher education. Although I worked primarily on two urban college campuses— far from the typically imagined “theaters of war”— my ﬁndings demonstrate how US imperialism was a deﬁnitive feature shaping college life in both set- tings. I show how students encountered US regimes of imperial racialization as part of their educational pathways and argue that localized systems of strati- ﬁed diﬀerence in Lahore and NYC are incorporated into the Global War on Terror and its attendant policies.

The chapters explore competing claims to inter- pret and appropriate the past and the major ethical issues associated with them, including handling the sacred; contested rights over sites, antiquities, and artifacts; the involvement of local communities in archaeological research; and the legal status of heritage sites. The Social Lives of the Elite: Friendship and Power in Pakistan Rosita Armytage The ways in which elite individuals perpetuate their power and privilege and so reinforce existing social inequalities within developing country contexts are analysed in this article. I argue that in highly politically and economically unstable environments, socialising between the uppermost bureaucratic, political, military and business elite serves to create intimacy and obligation between individuals who may be functionally useful to one another, and strengthens and reinforces elite privilege. In examining the motivations that drive the ways in which elites socialise, I contend that the blending of affective and instrumental relationships is reﬂective of the deep insecurity experienced by elites in contexts where they cannot expect their power and privilege to be upheld by the state. Keywords: Elites; Power; State Power; Instrumental Friendship; Social Inequality As we walk towards the stately, illuminated home of one of Islamabad’s most exclusive suburbs, trickles of laughter and music drift down to greet us.

Samina_Ahmed/Pakistan_s_Nuclear_Weapons_.author: Samina Ahmed
Samina_Ahmed/Pakistan_s_Nuclear_Weapons_.summary: Field sites: Anantnag. Turning Points and Nuclear Choices ~ ~ Pakistan tested a series of nuclear devices on May 28 and 30, 1998, signaling the abandonment of its policy of nuclear ambiguity, which it had adopted in the 1980s.' Under this policy, Pakistan had neither renounced nor acquired nuclear weapons for overt weaponization. The Pakistani action was motivated primarily by similar tests conducted in India on May 11 and 13, and was taken by Pakistan's nuclear weapons decisionmaking apparatus, comprising the military and the civil bureaucracy, including nuclear scientists. Despite a rigorous debate on the pros and cons of testing, Pakistan's political leadership played only a marginal role in determining Islamabad's response. Following the tests, Pakistan laid claim to the status of a nuclear weapons state, with Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif declaring, "No matter we are recognized as a nuclear weapons power or not, we are a nuclear power."' Pakistan's decision to test its nuclear capability represents a major turning point in its nuclear program.

Sana_Haroon/3___Religious_Revivalism_acr.summary: Field sites: Peshawar Division. 45 3 / Religious Revivalism across the Durand Line Sana Haroon I n the early twentieth century Afghanistan became a rallying point for anticolonial nationalists in British India, and between 1985 and 2001 it again became a rallying point, this time for Pakistani religious politics. In both cases, religious scholars (ulama) who called themselves Deobandi were engaged in projects in Afghanistan constructing a moral and authori- tative framework that drew on the pedagogies of Sunni revivalist Islam in an attempt to co-opt the moral legitimacy of the faith for the state. Spanning almost a century, the events that I describe in this chapter demonstrate, not so much a consistency of intent among the ulama east of the Durand Line or of the governments of Afghanistan, but instead the ways in which Afghani- stan and Pakistan have shared a history and a political economy of Islamic revivalism that is defi nitively anti-imperialist in its motivations. The Deobandi Ulama in Afghanistan Th rough the early twentieth century, the religious elites of Afghanistan worked in an uneasy accord with the government in Kabul.1 Afghan rul- ers attempted alternately to subordinate and appease the many…

With an increasing interest in fine arts, exhibitions and art shows were often held in major cities throughout the country where works of indigenous and foreign artists and calligraphers were displayed. Lyon uw Abstract: Since independence in 1947, highly politicised kinship practices have shaped the country from rural agricultural villages to the highest legislative and executive branches of government and the military. Ideal models of patrilineal affiliation have defined and guided patterns of factional loyalties. Although my earlier work has principally focused on village networks and politics, the same patterns of factional alliances can be seen at national levels to shed light on the activities of party poli­ tics.

Sudhir_Kakar/The_Inner_World__A_Psychoan.summary: Field sites: Hera. I like to think of this book as a contribution to social psychology in general and the social psychology of Hindu society in particular. Readers will quickly discover that I view social psychology as a study of the psychic representation in individuals of their society's culture and social institutions. This conception diverges somewhat from the dominant academic tradition in the subject which is rela- tively a-cultural and a-historical and is more concerned with studying the reactions of individuals in the 'here-and-now' situations of social stimulus. This book first began to take shape in a seminar 'Childhood and Society in India', which I gave at the Sigmund-Freud Institute of Psycho-analytic Training and Research in Frankfurt in the summer of 1972.

Wahid_Hussain/Educational_Anthropology__.author: Wahid Hussain
Wahid_Hussain/Educational_Anthropology__.summary: Field sites: Jammu. CITIZENSHIP IN INDIA Wahid Ahmad Dar and Irshad Ahmad Najar University of Kashmir, Srinagar, India abstract Despite much anthropological research on education in India, the importance of educational anthropology is not properly acknowledged. This article argues for fuller recognition of educational anthropology as a helpful tool to generate well- informed grassroots research throughout India. It connects this argument to concerns that education among tribal and other marginal communities reflects problems over acceptance of diversity. Educational anthropology could help to support sustainable, people-centric educational policies, curriculum construction, and above all better-focused teacher training.

Anila_Daulatzai/Acknowledging_Afghanista.title: Acknowledging Afghanistan: Notes and Queries on an Occupation
Anila_Daulatzai/Acknowledging_Afghanista.summary: Anila Daulatzai's article 'Acknowledging Afghanistan' offers a critical anthropological reflection on the post-2001 US occupation, drawing on her fieldwork with Afghan widows in Kabul. Daulatzai argues that humanitarian and counterinsurgency frames flatten Afghan ethical life. Field site: Kabul, Afghanistan. Methodology: ethnographic essay with theoretical argument. Anila_Daulatzai/The_Discursive_Occupatio.author: Anila Daulatzai
Anila_Daulatzai/The_Discursive_Occupatio.title: The Discursive Occupation of Afghanistan
Anila_Daulatzai/The_Discursive_Occupatio.summary: Anila Daulatzai's 'The Discursive Occupation of Afghanistan' critiques the framing of post-2001 Afghanistan in Western media and policy discourse, arguing that 'humanitarian' narratives obscure the realities of military occupation. Drawing on fieldwork in Kabul among widows and the urban poor, Daulatzai shows how discursive frames condition material intervention. Field site: Kabul, Afghanistan. Methodology: discourse analysis with ethnographic grounding. Published 2008.

Antonio_Giustozzi/The_Islamic_State_in_K.author: Antonio Giustozzi
Antonio_Giustozzi/The_Islamic_State_in_K.title: The Islamic State in Khorasan: Afghanistan, Pakistan and the New Central Asian Jihad
Antonio_Giustozzi/The_Islamic_State_in_K.summary: Antonio Giustozzi's The Islamic State in Khorasan documents the emergence and operation of ISKP across Afghanistan and Pakistan, drawing on field interviews with militants and Afghan security officials. The book maps the recruitment networks linking eastern Afghan provinces (Nangarhar, Kunar, Nuristan) to Pakistan's tribal areas and beyond. Field sites: Nangarhar, Kunar, Federally Administered Tribal Areas, Karachi. Methodology: militant and security-source interviews. Published 2018 by Hurst.

David_B_Edwards/Caravan_of_Martyrs__Sacr.author: David B Edwards
David_B_Edwards/Caravan_of_Martyrs__Sacr.title: Caravan of Martyrs: Sacrifice and Suicide Bombing in Afghanistan
David_B_Edwards/Caravan_of_Martyrs__Sacr.summary: David B. Edwards' Caravan of Martyrs traces how the Afghan jihad transformed cultural ideas of sacrifice, honor, and Pashtun tribalism into the logic of suicide bombing. Drawing on three decades of fieldwork in Pakistan's North-West Frontier and on audiovisual material produced by jihadi groups, Edwards argues that suicide bombing represents a rupture rather than a continuation of older martial traditions. Field site: Pashtun borderland, especially Peshawar and the tribal areas. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with media analysis. Published 2017 by University of California Press.

Christopher_Snedden/Independent_Kashmir_.author: Christopher Snedden
Christopher_Snedden/Independent_Kashmir_.title: Independent Kashmir: An Incomplete Aspiration
Christopher_Snedden/Independent_Kashmir_.summary: Christopher Snedden's Independent Kashmir traces the persistent aspiration for Kashmiri independence from 1846 through the post-2019 abrogation of Article 370, arguing that 'azadi' has remained politically alive across multiple constitutional regimes. Drawing on Indian, Pakistani, and Kashmiri sources, the book synthesizes narratives across all parts of the former princely state. Field sites: Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, Pakistan-administered Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan. Methodology: historical synthesis with interview material. Published 2021.

Robert_Wirsing/Fixing_Fractured_Nations_.title: Fixing Fractured Nations: The Challenge of Ethnic Separatism in the Asia-Pacific
Robert_Wirsing/Fixing_Fractured_Nations_.summary: Robert Wirsing's Fixing Fractured Nations gathers comparative case studies of ethnic separatism in the Asia-Pacific, with extensive treatment of Kashmir, Balochistan, and Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa. Wirsing argues that durable settlements require federal accommodation rather than security suppression. Field sites: comparative; Kashmir and Pakistan as central cases. Methodology: comparative political analysis. Published 2010 by Palgrave Macmillan.

Sumantra_Bose/Kashmir_at_the_Crossroads_.summary: Sumantra Bose's Kashmir at the Crossroads provides a comprehensive 21st-century history of the Kashmir conflict, with particular focus on the 2019 abrogation of Article 370 and its aftermath. Drawing on interviews with Kashmiri political figures and analysis of public documents, Bose situates the current crisis within seventy years of disputed sovereignty. Field site: Srinagar and the Kashmir Valley, with comparative reference to Azad Kashmir. Methodology: political analysis with interviews. Published 2021 by Yale University Press.

Karl_Jettmar/Antiquities_of_Northern_Pak.summary: Karl Jettmar's Antiquities of Northern Pakistan documents pre-Islamic rock carvings and inscriptions along the upper Indus and its tributaries from Chilas to Hunza, arguing that the region was a long-standing crossroads between South, Central, and East Asian religious traditions. The volumes catalogue Buddhist, Zoroastrian, Hindu, and shamanic motifs at sites including Hodar, Sazin, and Thalpan. Field sites: Chilas, Hodar, Sazin, Thalpan along the upper Indus, Pakistan. Methodology: archaeological survey and epigraphic analysis. Published 1989 onward by Philipp von Zabern.

Akbar_S_Ahmed/Millennium_and_Charisma_Am.title: Millennium and Charisma among Pathans: A Critical Essay in Social Anthropology
Akbar_S_Ahmed/Millennium_and_Charisma_Am.summary: Akbar S. Ahmed's Millennium and Charisma among Pathans is an ethnographic and theoretical study of millenarian Sufi movements among Pukhtuns in Pakistan's North-West Frontier, focusing on the Akbarid uprising in Swat. The book argues for a structural-functional reading of charismatic leadership that rejects Barth's individualist transactional model. Field sites: Swat, Mohmand, Pakistani Pukhtun tribal areas. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork and historical reconstruction. Published 1976 by Routledge & Kegan Paul.

Ather_Zia/A_Desolation_Called_Peace__Voi.title: A Desolation Called Peace: Voices from Kashmir
Ather_Zia/A_Desolation_Called_Peace__Voi.summary: A Desolation Called Peace, edited by Ather Zia and Javaid Iqbal Bhat, gathers essays, poems, and testimonies from Kashmiri writers documenting life under Indian military occupation. The volume combines literary and ethnographic registers to record voices from Srinagar, Kupwara, and Pulwama. Field sites: Kashmir Valley. Methodology: edited literary-ethnographic anthology. Published 2019 by HarperCollins India.

Ather_Zia/Resisting_Disappearance__452d8.author: Ather Zia
Ather_Zia/Resisting_Disappearance__452d8.title: Resisting Disappearance: Military Occupation and Women's Activism in Kashmir
Ather_Zia/Resisting_Disappearance__452d8.summary: Ather Zia's Resisting Disappearance is an ethnography of the Association of Parents of Disappeared Persons (APDP) in Kashmir, focusing on the half-widows and mothers who pursue missing relatives across decades of Indian military occupation. Zia argues that 'affective justice work' constitutes a distinct form of women's political agency. Field site: Srinagar and the Kashmir Valley. Methodology: long-term participant observation with APDP. Published 2019 by University of Washington Press.

Sana_Haroon/The_Mosques_of_Colonial_Sout.title: The Mosques of Colonial South Asia: A Social and Legal History of Muslim Worship
Sana_Haroon/The_Mosques_of_Colonial_Sout.summary: Sana Haroon's The Mosques of Colonial South Asia is a legal and social history of mosque construction, sect dispute, and congregational practice in late-colonial India and Pakistan. Drawing on Indian and British court records, Haroon shows how colonial law constructed Muslim 'community' through property disputes. Field sites: Punjab, Sindh, North-West Frontier, and United Provinces. Methodology: legal and archival history. Published 2021 by Cambridge University Press.

Magnus_Marsden/Living_Islam__Muslim_Reli.author: Magnus Marsden
Magnus_Marsden/Living_Islam__Muslim_Reli.title: Living Islam: Muslim Religious Experience in Pakistan's North-West Frontier
Magnus_Marsden/Living_Islam__Muslim_Reli.summary: Magnus Marsden's Living Islam is a long-term ethnography of Muslim religious life in Chitral, in Pakistan's North-West Frontier (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), arguing against narratives that reduce frontier Islam to militancy. Marsden documents Sunni-Ismaili-Shia debate, poetry recitation, and Sufi discipleship across Chitrali villages. Field sites: Chitral District (Rowshan, Markaz), Pakistan. Methodology: extended ethnographic fieldwork. Published 2005 by Cambridge University Press.

Nivi_Manchanda/Imagining_Afghanistan__Th.title: Imagining Afghanistan: The History and Politics of Imperial Knowledge
Nivi_Manchanda/Imagining_Afghanistan__Th.summary: Nivi Manchanda's Imagining Afghanistan analyzes how Western scholarly and popular knowledge has constructed Afghanistan as a tribal, ungovernable space, tracing this imaginary from 19th-century British imperial writing through 21st-century counterinsurgency analysis. The book combines critical international relations theory with archival reading. Field sites: textual and archival; Afghanistan as object of knowledge. Methodology: critical genealogy of imperial knowledge. Published 2020 by Cambridge University Press.

Christine_Fair/Fighting_to_the_End__The_.author: Christine Fair
Christine_Fair/Fighting_to_the_End__The_.title: Fighting to the End: The Pakistan Army's Way of War
Christine_Fair/Fighting_to_the_End__The_.summary: Christine Fair's Fighting to the End argues that the Pakistan Army's strategic culture treats the existential rivalry with India as the decisive frame for all foreign and domestic policy, drawing on a systematic content analysis of Pakistani military journals. Fair's argument explains why the army maintains militant proxies despite their costs. Field site: Pakistan (military institutional analysis, Rawalpindi, Islamabad). Methodology: content analysis of Pakistani military doctrinal literature. Published 2014 by Oxford University Press.

Mubbashir_Rizvi/The_Ethics_of_Staying__S.summary: Mubbashir Rizvi's The Ethics of Staying is an ethnography of the Anjuman Mazareen Punjab tenant movement in Okara, Punjab, where peasants resist Pakistan Army efforts to convert occupancy tenancy into corporate leases. Rizvi argues that the slogan 'malki ya maut' (ownership or death) articulates a vernacular ethics of place. Field site: Okara military farms, Punjab, Pakistan. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with tenant activists. Published 2019 by Stanford University Press.

Sonia_Ahsan_Tirmizi/Pious_Peripheries__R.summary: Sonia Ahsan-Tirmizi's Pious Peripheries is an ethnography of women's shelters in Kabul, where 'runaway' women — those fleeing forced marriage or domestic violence — negotiate Islamic ethics, state law, and donor expectations. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with shelter residents and staff. Published 2021 by Stanford University Press.

Fredrik_Barth/Ethnic_Groups_and_Boundari.summary: Fredrik Barth's Ethnic Groups and Boundaries reframes ethnicity as the maintenance of social boundaries rather than the content of cultural traits, with case studies including the Pathans of Pakistan and Afghanistan. Barth's introduction proposes that boundaries persist despite cross-boundary flow of people and practices. Field sites: Swat (Pakistan) and other comparative cases. Methodology: theoretical synthesis with ethnographic case studies. Published 1969 by Allen & Unwin.

Ahmed's structural-functional critique of Barth's transactional model of Pukhtun social organization. Akbar_Ahmed/Pukhtun_Economy_and_Society_.summary: Akbar S. Ahmed's Pukhtun Economy and Society documents social and economic transformation among the Mohmand of Pakistan's North-West Frontier, contrasting nang (honor-based) and qalang (rent-based) modes of social organization. Drawing on Ahmed's service as Political Agent, the book argues that Pukhtun society maintains distinctive economic logics under modernization. Field site: Mohmand Agency, FATA, Pakistan. Methodology: anthropological fieldwork with administrative experience. Published 1980 by Routledge & Kegan Paul.

Adamec's six-volume Historical and Political Gazetteer of Afghanistan reissues the British Indian Army's 1914 confidential gazetteer with extensive scholarly annotation. Tariq_Rahman/Pakistan_s_Wars__An_Alterna.title: Pakistan's Wars: An Alternative History
Tariq_Rahman/Pakistan_s_Wars__An_Alterna.summary: Tariq Rahman's Pakistan's Wars: An Alternative History reconstructs the major Pakistani wars (1947-48, 1965, 1971, Kargil 1999, post-9/11 frontier wars) from a non-establishment Pakistani perspective, drawing on Urdu memoirs and Pakistani veteran testimony. Field sites: Punjab, Kashmir LoC, FATA. Methodology: synthetic military-political history. Published 2022 by Vanguard Books.

Victoria_Schofield/Afghan_Frontier__Feud.title: Afghan Frontier: Feuding and Fighting in Central Asia
Victoria_Schofield/Afghan_Frontier__Feud.summary: Victoria Schofield's Afghan Frontier traces 200 years of Anglo-Afghan and Anglo-Russian rivalry in Afghanistan and the Pashtun frontier, drawing on British archival sources and Schofield's earlier reportage in Pakistan. Field sites: Khyber, eastern Afghanistan, NWFP. Methodology: narrative history. Published 2003 by I.B. Tauris.

Saiba_Varma/The_Occupied_Clinic__bc34f6c.author: Saiba Varma
Saiba_Varma/The_Occupied_Clinic__bc34f6c.title: The Occupied Clinic: Militarism and Care in Kashmir
Saiba_Varma/The_Occupied_Clinic__bc34f6c.summary: Saiba Varma's The Occupied Clinic is an ethnography of psychiatric and medical care in the Kashmir Valley under Indian military occupation, arguing that medicine and militarism are co-constituted rather than separate domains. Drawing on long-term fieldwork in hospitals, clinics, and homes in Srinagar and surrounding districts, Varma shows how counterinsurgency reshapes how Kashmiris experience care, suffering, and trust. Field site: Srinagar and the Kashmir Valley, India-administered Jammu and Kashmir. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with patients, psychiatrists, and security personnel. Published 2020 by Duke University Press.

Naveeda_Khan/Muslim_Becoming_Aspiration_.author: Naveeda Khan
Naveeda_Khan/Muslim_Becoming_Aspiration_.title: Muslim Becoming: Aspiration and Skepticism in Pakistan
Naveeda_Khan/Muslim_Becoming_Aspiration_.summary: Naveeda Khan's Muslim Becoming examines theological argument and everyday Islam in urban Pakistan, arguing that ordinary Muslims approach faith through aspiration and skepticism rather than fixed doctrine. The book traces sectarian disputes and Sufi-influenced practice in Lahore and other Punjabi cities, drawing on extended ethnographic fieldwork and on close reading of Urdu polemical literature. Field site: Lahore, Punjab, Pakistan. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork combined with vernacular textual analysis. Published 2012 by Duke University Press.

Hafsa_Kanjwal/Colonizing_Kashmir_State_B.author: Hafsa Kanjwal
Hafsa_Kanjwal/Colonizing_Kashmir_State_B.title: Colonizing Kashmir: State-Building under Indian Occupation
Hafsa_Kanjwal/Colonizing_Kashmir_State_B.summary: Hafsa Kanjwal's Colonizing Kashmir argues that postcolonial Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir constitutes a settler-colonial project, with Bakshi Ghulam Mohammad's 1953-63 government as a constitutive phase of state-building. Based on archival research in Indian and Kashmiri archives plus oral histories, the book documents how infrastructure, tourism, education, and emergency law produced consent and coercion in the Valley. Field site: Srinagar, Kashmir Valley, and Indian state archives. Methodology: archival history with oral history interviews. Published 2023 by Stanford University Press.

Humeira_Iqtidar/Secularizing_Islamists_I.author: Humeira Iqtidar
Humeira_Iqtidar/Secularizing_Islamists_I.title: Secularizing Islamists? Jamaat-e-Islami and Jamaat-ud-Dawa in Urban Pakistan
Humeira_Iqtidar/Secularizing_Islamists_I.summary: Humeira Iqtidar's Secularizing Islamists argues that Pakistani Islamist parties Jamaat-e-Islami and Jamaat-ud-Dawa, far from being a counter-secular force, have themselves contributed to secularization in Lahore by detaching religion from custom and embedding it in state politics. The book draws on ethnographic fieldwork inside both organizations. Field site: Lahore, Pakistan. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with Islamist activists. Published 2011 by University of Chicago Press.

Cabeiri_Robinson/Body_of_Victim_Body_of_.author: Cabeiri Robinson
Cabeiri_Robinson/Body_of_Victim_Body_of_.title: Body of Victim, Body of Warrior: Refugee Families and the Making of Kashmiri Jihadists
Cabeiri_Robinson/Body_of_Victim_Body_of_.summary: Cabeiri D. Robinson's Body of Victim, Body of Warrior is an ethnography of Kashmiri refugee families in Azad Jammu and Kashmir whose sons have joined cross-LoC militant groups. Robinson argues that Kashmiri jihad must be understood through the moral economy of muhajir refugee status and family honor rather than through Pakistani state recruitment alone. Field site: Muzaffarabad and Mirpur, Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Methodology: long-term ethnographic fieldwork. Published 2013 by University of California Press.

Antonio_Giustozzi/Koran_Kalashnikov_Lapt.author: Antonio Giustozzi
Antonio_Giustozzi/Koran_Kalashnikov_Lapt.title: Koran, Kalashnikov, and Laptop: The Neo-Taliban Insurgency in Afghanistan
Antonio_Giustozzi/Koran_Kalashnikov_Lapt.summary: Antonio Giustozzi's Koran, Kalashnikov, and Laptop maps the rebuilding of the Taliban movement after 2001, tracing recruitment, financing, and tactical adaptation across southern and eastern Afghanistan. The book draws on field interviews with insurgent commanders and ANA personnel. Field sites: Kandahar, Helmand, Uruzgan, Zabul, eastern border provinces. Methodology: militant and security-source interviews. Published 2008 by Hurst.

David_B_Edwards/Heroes_of_the_Age_Moral_.author: David B Edwards
David_B_Edwards/Heroes_of_the_Age_Moral_.title: Heroes of the Age: Moral Fault Lines on the Afghan Frontier
David_B_Edwards/Heroes_of_the_Age_Moral_.summary: David B. Edwards' Heroes of the Age is a foundational anthropological history of Afghan moral imagination centered on three iconic figures: a Pashtun tribal saint, an Amir, and a Marxist intellectual. Edwards argues that competing models of legitimate authority — tribe, state, and revolution — have structured Afghan political life since the late 19th century. Field sites: eastern Afghan/Pakistan borderland (Pukhtun tribal areas, Peshawar, Kabul). Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork combined with biographical history. Published 1996 by University of California Press.

Mike_Martin/Intimate_War_Helmand_Conflic.author: Mike Martin
Mike_Martin/Intimate_War_Helmand_Conflic.title: An Intimate War: An Oral History of the Helmand Conflict, 1978-2012
Mike_Martin/Intimate_War_Helmand_Conflic.summary: Mike Martin's An Intimate War is an oral history of the Helmand conflict from the 1978 communist coup through the 2012 NATO drawdown, drawing on Pashto-language interviews Martin conducted as a British army officer. The book argues that the conflict's drivers were intra-tribal and tribal-state rather than ideological, and that Western framings of 'Taliban' obscure this. Field site: Helmand Province, Afghanistan. Methodology: oral history with Helmandi informants. Published 2014 by Hurst.

Olivier_Roy/Islam_and_Resistance_in_Afgh.author: Olivier Roy
Olivier_Roy/Islam_and_Resistance_in_Afgh.title: Islam and Resistance in Afghanistan
Olivier_Roy/Islam_and_Resistance_in_Afgh.summary: Olivier Roy's Islam and Resistance in Afghanistan is the foundational political-anthropological account of the anti-Soviet mujahideen, arguing that the resistance was structured by older Sufi networks and tribal segmentation rather than by Islamist ideology imported from Egypt. Roy draws on extended fieldwork in Pakistan-based mujahideen camps and inside Afghanistan. Field sites: Peshawar mujahideen camps, eastern Afghan provinces (Nuristan, Kunar, Panjshir). Methodology: political ethnography. Published 1986 by Cambridge University Press.

Dipali_Mukhopadhyay/Mukhopadhyay_Warlord.author: Dipali Mukhopadhyay
Dipali_Mukhopadhyay/Mukhopadhyay_Warlord.title: Warlords, Strongman Governors, and the State in Afghanistan
Dipali_Mukhopadhyay/Mukhopadhyay_Warlord.summary: Dipali Mukhopadhyay's Warlords, Strongman Governors, and the State in Afghanistan traces how former mujahideen and anti-Taliban militia leaders re-entered state office as provincial governors after 2001, arguing that these 'strongman governors' produced a hybrid order rather than obstructing state-building. Drawing on field interviews with governors including Atta Mohammad Noor (Balkh) and Gul Agha Sherzai (Nangarhar), the book argues for re-evaluating informal authority. Field sites: Mazar-i-Sharif (Balkh), Jalalabad (Nangarhar), Herat. Methodology: elite political ethnography. Published 2014 by Cambridge University Press.

Goldie_Osuri/Osuri_Religious_Freedom_Ind.author: Goldie Osuri
Goldie_Osuri/Osuri_Religious_Freedom_Ind.title: Religious Freedom in India: Sovereignty and (Anti) Conversion
Goldie_Osuri/Osuri_Religious_Freedom_Ind.summary: Goldie Osuri's Religious Freedom in India argues that anti-conversion debates and Hindutva mobilization reveal a fundamental Indian state ambivalence about minority religious sovereignty, with particular attention to Adivasi, Christian, and Kashmiri Muslim communities. The book combines critical theory with discourse analysis. Field sites: textual and policy; Indian-administered Kashmir as recurring case. Methodology: critical political theory. Published 2013 by Routledge.

Christopher_Snedden/Understanding_Kashmi.author: Christopher Snedden
Christopher_Snedden/Understanding_Kashmi.title: Understanding Kashmir and Kashmiris
Christopher_Snedden/Understanding_Kashmi.summary: Christopher Snedden's Understanding Kashmir and Kashmiris synthesizes the political, religious, and ethnic complexity of all the entities of the former princely state — Indian-administered J&K, Pakistan-administered Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, and Chinese-controlled Aksai Chin and the Trans-Karakoram Tract. The book draws on extended fieldwork across the divided Kashmir region. Field sites: Srinagar, Jammu, Muzaffarabad, Gilgit, Skardu. Methodology: historical and political synthesis with interviews. Published 2015 by Hurst.

Suvir_Kaul/Of_Gardens_Graves_Kashmir_Kau.author: Suvir Kaul
Suvir_Kaul/Of_Gardens_Graves_Kashmir_Kau.title: Of Gardens and Graves: Kashmir, Poetry, Politics
Suvir_Kaul/Of_Gardens_Graves_Kashmir_Kau.summary: Suvir Kaul's Of Gardens and Graves reads contemporary Kashmiri poetry and political essays as testimony to the everyday violence of Indian military occupation in the Kashmir Valley. The book translates and analyzes Kashmiri and Urdu poetry by writers such as Agha Shahid Ali, Naseem Shafaie, and others. Field site: Kashmir Valley (textual and visited). Methodology: literary criticism with political reflection. Published 2015 by Three Essays Collective.

Sumantra_Bose/Kashmir_Roots_of_Conflict_.summary: Sumantra Bose's Kashmir: Roots of Conflict, Paths to Peace traces the dispute from 1846 through the 2002 Indian elections, arguing that durable peace requires recognition of Kashmiri political agency and federal accommodation across the LoC. The book draws on Indian, Pakistani, and Kashmiri sources plus extensive fieldwork. Field sites: Srinagar, Jammu, Azad Kashmir. Methodology: political-historical analysis with interviews. Max_Klimburg/Klimburg_Kafirs_Hindu_Kush_.summary: Max Klimburg's The Kafirs of the Hindu Kush documents the ritual, art, and material culture of the pre-Islamic Kafir communities of the Waigal and Ashkun valleys of Nuristan, drawing on Klimburg's fieldwork before the Afghan wars. The two-volume work catalogues wooden effigies, dance ritual, and lineage organization. Field sites: Waigal and Ashkun valleys, Nuristan, Afghanistan. Methodology: ethnography combined with art-historical documentation. Published 1999 by Franz Steiner.

Bhan argues that 'tribal authenticity' is mobilized by the state to incorporate borderland populations into national identity while justifying military presence. Field site: Dah-Hanu and Drass, Ladakh. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork. Published 2014 by Routledge.

Lindholm argues that the ostensible egalitarianism of Pukhtun lineage competition is sustained by intense distrust between agnatic cousins, with hospitality as its public counterpoise. Field site: Swat valley, Pakistan. Methodology: long-term ethnographic fieldwork. Published 1982 by Columbia University Press.

Anna_Larson/Larson_Afghanistan_democracy.title: Derailing Democracy in Afghanistan: Elections in an Unstable Political Landscape
Anna_Larson/Larson_Afghanistan_democracy.summary: Noah Coburn (Bennington College) and Anna Larson's joint ethnography of post-2001 Afghan elections, published 2013 by Columbia University Press. The book argues that internationally-funded elections, instead of democratising Afghanistan, entrenched local strongmen and produced a brittle 'electoral landscape' that international donors badly misread. Field sites: Kabul; Istalif (Shomali Plain); Hazarajat; and provinces across Balkh, Logar, and Ghazni during the 2009 presidential and 2010 parliamentary elections. Methodology: multi-sited ethnographic fieldwork in polling stations, campaign offices, and tribal councils, plus elite interviews.

Max_Klimburg/Kafirs_of_the_Hindu_Kush__4.summary: Max Klimburg's The Kafirs of the Hindu Kush documents the ritual, art, and material culture of the pre-Islamic Kafir communities of the Waigal and Ashkun valleys of Nuristan, drawing on Klimburg's fieldwork before the Afghan wars. Bhan argues that 'tribal authenticity' is mobilized by the state to incorporate borderland populations into national identity while justifying military presence. Field site: Dah-Hanu and Drass, Ladakh. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork. Published 2014 by Routledge.

Sana_Haroon/Frontier_of_Faith_Islam_in_t.summary: Sana Haroon's Frontier of Faith traces the role of Sunni Deobandi networks in the Pakistan-Afghanistan tribal frontier from the late 19th century through the 1947 Partition, arguing that mosques and madrasas formed durable institutional infrastructure independent of the colonial state. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork with shelter residents and staff. Published 2021 by Stanford University Press.

Inshah_Malik/Inshah_Malik_Muslim_Women_K.title: Muslim Women, Agency and Resistance Politics: The Case of Kashmir
Inshah_Malik/Inshah_Malik_Muslim_Women_K.summary: Inshah Malik's Muslim Women, Agency and Resistance Politics is an ethnography of Kashmiri women's political agency from Dukhtaran-e-Millat to the post-2008 Awam Movement, arguing for a vocabulary of resistance grounded in Muslim ethics rather than secular feminism. Conrad_Schetter/Local_Politics_Afghanist.author: Conrad Schetter
Conrad_Schetter/Local_Politics_Afghanist.title: Local Politics in Afghanistan: A Century of Intervention in the Social Order
Conrad_Schetter/Local_Politics_Afghanist.summary: Conrad Schetter's edited Local Politics in Afghanistan brings together German and Anglo political-anthropological work documenting how external interventions reshape Afghan local social order, with chapters on Pashtun, Tajik, and Uzbek rural districts. Schetter argues that 'the local' is produced through these interventions rather than existing prior to them. Field sites: rural Afghanistan (Kandahar, Balkh, Kunduz, Bamyan). Methodology: edited political-ethnographic essays. Published 2013 by Hurst.

Adam_Baczko/Taliban_Courts_in_Afghanista.author: Adam Baczko
Adam_Baczko/Taliban_Courts_in_Afghanista.title: The Taliban Courts in Afghanistan: Waging War by Law
Adam_Baczko/Taliban_Courts_in_Afghanista.summary: Adam Baczko's English-language reworking (translated by Henry W. Randolph) of his 2021 La Guerre par le Droit, published by Oxford University Press in 2023. The book argues that the Taliban built sustained popular legitimacy in rural Afghanistan by running parallel sharia courts that resolved everyday land, inheritance, and water disputes more reliably than Karzai-era state institutions. Field sites: rural districts of Wardak, Kunar, Kandahar, Logar, Ghazni; with secondary work among Afghan refugees in Quetta, Pakistan. Methodology: long-term ethnographic fieldwork (2010–2018) with disputants, judges, and former Taliban personnel, plus archival reconstruction of the Taliban judiciary's emergence.

Zoha_Waseem/Insecure_Guardians_Everyday_.author: Zoha Waseem
Zoha_Waseem/Insecure_Guardians_Everyday_.title: Insecure Guardians: Enforcement, Encounters and Everyday Policing in Postcolonial Karachi
Zoha_Waseem/Insecure_Guardians_Everyday_.summary: Zoha Waseem's ethnography of the Karachi Police, published 2022 by Hurst (London) and Oxford University Press. Based on multi-year fieldwork inside police stations, encounter sites, and ranger compounds, the book argues that policing in Karachi is an inherently insecure profession: officers are simultaneously agents and victims of routinised violence, embedded in a postcolonial security apparatus shaped by Sindh's ethnic politics, MQM-era extrajudicial encounters, and the post-2013 Karachi Operation. Field sites: Karachi (Lyari, Malir, Korangi, North Nazimabad). Methodology: ethnography, life-history interviews with constables and officers, archival policing-record analysis. Developed from her King's College London PhD.

Humeira_Iqtidar/Secularizing_Islamists_J.author: Humeira Iqtidar
Humeira_Iqtidar/Secularizing_Islamists_J.title: Secularizing Islamists? Jama'at-e-Islami and Jama'at-ud-Da'wa in Urban Pakistan
Humeira_Iqtidar/Secularizing_Islamists_J.summary: Humeira Iqtidar's monograph (University of Chicago Press, 2011, South Asia Across the Disciplines series) argues counter-intuitively that two prominent Islamist organisations — Jama'at-e-Islami and Jama'at-ud-Da'wa — have been agents of secularisation in urban Pakistan, professionalising religion through bureaucratic structures, mass media, and welfare provision rather than restoring an organic religious order. Field sites: Lahore neighbourhoods (Krishan Nagar, Iqbal Town, Township) and Markaz-e-Tayyaba in Muridke, with secondary observation in Karachi. Methodology: ethnographic fieldwork (2003–2008), party document analysis, interviews with cadres and sympathisers.

Anna_Larson/Power_and_Authority_in_Afgha.author: Anna Larson
Anna_Larson/Power_and_Authority_in_Afgha.title: Power and Authority in Afghanistan: Rethinking Politics, Intervention and Rule
Anna_Larson/Power_and_Authority_in_Afgha.summary: An edited volume from Anna Larson (Tufts/AIIS), Dipali Mukhopadhyay (Minnesota), and Omar Sharifi (Boston University), published 2025 by I.B. Tauris/Bloomsbury. Twelve chapters by Afghan and international scholars rethink power and political authority in Afghanistan after the 2021 Taliban return, arguing that 'intervention' and 'rule' need to be re-theorised away from Western state-building templates. Field sites: Kabul, Kandahar, Bamiyan/Hazarajat, Mazar-e Sharif, Herat, Logar, and the Pakistani borderlands of Quetta and Peshawar. Methodology: edited ethnographic and historical-political case studies; the editors' own chapters draw on long-term fieldwork stretching back to the post-2001 reconstruction era.

Salma_Bibi/Gendered_Landscape_of_Justice.author: Salma Bibi
Salma_Bibi/Gendered_Landscape_of_Justice.title: The Gendered Landscape of Justice: Institutional Barriers to Women's Khula Rights in District Courts Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Salma_Bibi/Gendered_Landscape_of_Justice.summary: Salma Bibi (PhD scholar, Department of Social Work, University of Peshawar) and Shakeel Ahmed analyse how patriarchal gatekeeping inside Peshawar's district family courts blocks women from invoking their Islamic right to khula (judicial divorce). Field site: Peshawar District family courts and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa civil society. Methodology: qualitative interviews with female litigants, lawyers, and judges, framed by feminist structural-oppression theory (Maeve McKeown). Published 2025 in the Journal of Social Sciences Review 5(1):267–276.

Rahat_Ullah/Access_to_Justice_in_Land_Di.author: Rahat Ullah
Rahat_Ullah/Access_to_Justice_in_Land_Di.title: Access to Justice in Land Disputes: Unveiling Public Challenges in Peshawar Courts
Rahat_Ullah/Access_to_Justice_in_Land_Di.summary: Rahat Ullah (LLM, Kohat University) and Salma Bibi (PhD, University of Peshawar) diagnose why land-dispute litigation in Peshawar's civil and revenue courts drags on for years and erodes public trust. Field site: civil and revenue courts of Peshawar, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. Methodology: qualitative analysis of 30 purposively selected respondents — judges, revenue officers, senior advocates, and litigants — to map the structural, procedural, and administrative barriers to timely justice under the West Pakistan Land Revenue Act 1967 and the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. Published 2025 in Social Science Review Archives 3(4).

Ghazala_Hassan_Qadri/A_Muslim_Womans_Rig.author: Ghazala Hassan Qadri
Ghazala_Hassan_Qadri/A_Muslim_Womans_Rig.title: A Muslim Woman's Right to a Khul' in Pakistan: Marital Relief or Marital Pain?
Ghazala_Hassan_Qadri/A_Muslim_Womans_Rig.summary: Ghazala Hassan Qadri's PhD thesis (University of Birmingham, Department of Theology and Religion, submitted November 2016, accepted 2017) re-examines the Hanafi jurisprudence of khul' — the woman-initiated divorce — and tracks its translation into the Pakistani legal system. Qadri argues that earlier scholarship misread Hanafi fiqh as requiring the husband's consent and a financial penalty, and shows how Pakistani courts have effectively created a no-fault khul' through judicial activism. Field site: Lahore family courts. Methodology: doctrinal fiqh analysis, statutory review, plus qualitative interviews and participant observation with female litigants and judges in Lahore.

Shabana_Shamaas_Gul_Khattak/Voices_of_th.author: Shabana Shamaas Gul Khattak
Shabana_Shamaas_Gul_Khattak/Voices_of_th.title: Voices of the Unvoiced: Women's Struggle for Education in Khyber Pukhtunkhwa, Pakistan
Shabana_Shamaas_Gul_Khattak/Voices_of_th.summary: Shabana Shamaas Gul Khattak's book-length study of women's pursuit of formal education across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, published 2025 by Anthem Press (London/New York; distributed via Cambridge Core). The book documents how Pashtun gender norms, post-9/11 militancy, the 2009 Swat displacement, and KP's underfunded public schools combine to produce structural barriers — and how local women, teachers, and NGOs work around them. Field sites: Swat, Peshawar, Mardan, Charsadda, and Malakand division. Methodology: feminist ethnography, oral histories with school-girls, mothers, and women teachers, plus local-government archival work.

Maira_Hayat/Storage_as_Security_Damming_.author: Maira Hayat
Maira_Hayat/Storage_as_Security_Damming_.title: Storage as Security: Damming Water in Pakistan
Maira_Hayat/Storage_as_Security_Damming_.summary: Maira Hayat's short essay in Political Geography (2022) examines how Pakistani elites — including former Chief Justice Saqib Nisar — frame large dam construction (Diamer-Bhasha, Mohmand, Mangla, Tarbela) as a moral and security imperative against Indian water-bombing fears. Field site: Lahore (engineering academies); analytic site: Pakistan's dam infrastructure on the Indus. Methodology: ethnographic vignettes and discourse analysis of public-fundraising appeals. Published 2022 in Political Geography 97 (Suppl C), DOI 10.1016/j.polgeo.2022.102629.
